This looks like a good start. A useful feature can be to permit a second argument to `import.meta.resolve` that allows providing a different baseURL for the resolution function - this lets `import.meta.resolve` behave both as a contextual resolver and as a more general resolver as well.

I can provide some spec along these lines if you'd be open to it?
I'd like to get the basic version out there first. Adding more features is a sure way to prevent this one from landing.
In principle this sounds reasonable to me. Would also like to hear from @jasnell, @lucacasonato, and @codehag. Do we have some kind of place where we document extensions to `import.meta`?
I guess we have https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/import.meta ?
Yeah, I'm +1 on this. It'll be quite useful, I think.
I have no strong opinion (maybe +0.1?). Not opposed, but I know some Node folks want this to be async. We are fine with it being sync (and would want it to be sync).
I don't see an issue with introducing this. I think this would be useful to test import maps, and i imagine it will be useful in such a world were import maps are the norm?

Awesome, thanks all for the review. I'll plan to merge this after I'm a bit more confident in the tests; I have some up initially at https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/3456729 but that CL is messy enough that I don't trust them yet.

Hey, can we slow this down just a bit? I’m a bit concerned with this being sync, since in Node the resolution step is async (and needs to remain so, or it would break various loaders use cases).

Taking a step back, for the non-bare case isn’t `import.meta.resolve("./foo.txt")` the same as `new URL("./foo.txt", import.meta.url)`? What’s the advantage of `import.meta.resolve`?

And the bare case, `import.meta.resolve("somepackage/resource.json")`, depends on import maps? Is there any anticipation that in the future the resolution of `somepackage` might be something that happens dynamically, similar to Node’s loaders? And if so, perhaps `import.meta.resolve` would need to be an async function so that this future dynamic resolution could take advantage of things like network calls?

I think a 7-month incubation period is slow enough?

It's ok for Node to use a different API than the web here.

This is different than the URL constructor because import maps, indeed. There is no plan to make that async; we never want to introduce network calls into module resolution on the web.

Put another way, is there some advantage in making this sync? If it’s async then we can maintain compatibility with Node or any platform that wants to allow customization in module resolution (and for that custom resolution to potentially be async).

@domenic This issue was raised 7 months back by the Node folks already (although not in this thread - see https://github.com/nodejs/modules/issues/550#issuecomment-685146852).

I am really not in favor of this turning into another `setTimeout` where the web and Node have different return value. If it is looks like this may be the case, Deno is in strict opposition.

> @domenic This issue was raised 7 months back by the Node folks already (although not in this thread - see [nodejs/modules#550 (comment)](https://github.com/nodejs/modules/issues/550#issuecomment-685146852)).

There’s also extensive discussion in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/3871. There are many Node folks on that thread asking for this to be async. There are also arguments for this to be async to support dynamically-loaded import maps.

Yeah, I suggest Node not implement this if they can't make it sync; that's what I meant above. They can implement a different API.

On the web the benefit of it being sync is the same as the benefit of URL resolution being sync.

I agree this was already discussed extensively and the conclusion hasn't changed.

One of the motivations for this API was to have a resolution syntax that was statically analyzable across platforms, including Node and Deno. See https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/7296#issuecomment-685143284. If an API is chosen that Node can’t implement, that goal would not be achieved.

Another use case was dynamically loaded import maps; see https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/3871#issuecomment-632368537. This would also require an async API. My reading of #3871 did not leave me with the impression that a consensus had been reached.

It seems like the motivation for landing this now is to make import maps easier to test in the browser. That’s a worthy goal, but perhaps an API specific to import maps could be designed? And `import.meta.resolve`, as a way of querying the current platform’s module resolution algorithm, could be designed in a way that is cross-platform.

Edit: Node already has an experimental async `import.meta.resolve`: https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html#importmetaresolvespecifier-parent

I'd be +1 on making this API return a Promise. It's fairly trivial to have `import.meta.resolve()` import a synchronously resolved Promise in the cases where async is not strictly necessary. I don't really see the value in ruling out a class of potential use cases, or intentionally designing the API so that it doesn't work for one of the major implementers when it can be easily avoided.

I maintain that it's OK for non-web platforms and web platforms to diverge. Recall this is a body for standardizing web APIs; if other platforms want to follow, they can, but they're not obligated to.

I'm curious what other browser implementers think about that. If that's not acceptable to them then I plan to abandon this effort, as I'm not willing to constrain our API design in that way. Other platforms making the choice to design their module system in a way that makes effectively-URL-resolution async is not an acceptable constraint on the web's module system and would strongly discourage me from further investing in the web's module system at all if it became one.

In that case we'd work through the other test-only API options for testing import maps. (Although I would not spend any further effort on import maps personally, after cleaning up our testing debt, due to this new constraint.)

> Another use case was dynamically loaded import maps; see https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/3871#issuecomment-632368537. This would also require an async API.

This is not correct; the API can return the resolution value at the time, based on the currently-loaded import maps. It doesn't have to (and in fact won't) block on network.

Perhaps there could be two APIs, one for resolving per import maps and one that queries the current platform’s module resolution algorithm? So like `import.meta.importMapResolve` could be sync and could return the resolution value based on the currently-loaded import maps, and `import.meta.resolve` would be the API that Node has in https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html#importmetaresolvespecifier-parent. This would seem to satisfy both use cases, in that `import.meta.importMapResolve` would provide a sync way to resolve bare specifiers (just as `new URL` provides a sync way to resolve relative paths) and an async `import.meta.resolve` could be a cross-platform-compatible way to do module resolution.
I don't think `importMapResolve` is an appropriate name for the web platform's import resolution algorithm. I agree Node could have two APIs, but on the web we only have one such algorithm.

@domenic :
> I maintain that it's OK for non-web platforms and web platforms to diverge.

Let's make sure we're being clear here. When you say "The Web", you mean "Web Browsers". The Web is more than just Browsers these days. That said, non-Browser vs. Browser is not really the point here. End users (developers using the APIs in this case) want to be able to write code that works consistently across multiple environments, regardless of whether it is running on the Web in a browser, running on the Web on the edge, or running on the Web on a server. It ought to be more than possible for us to develop reasonable APIs that meet that desire. I think we all agree that it is OK for platforms of different types to diverge *when necessary* but it also makes a whole lot of sense (and delivers a whole lot of value to the ecosystem) for us to *avoid divergence when possible* when those different platforms need to accomplish the same things.  But I'll leave this soapbox for another venue...

@domenic:
> ... is not an acceptable constraint on the web's module system...

Assuming I'm missing something fundamental so here's a question: How does having this API return a `Promise` (that can be resolved synchronously) unreasonably constrain this API or implementations of it? Having it return a Promise does not require that platforms implement async resolution by any stretch of the imagination. By way of example of another spec, the Cloudflare Worker's Web Crypto API implementation returns Promises as spec'd but returns immediately resolved promises. Sure, it adds the additional continuation step in the microtask queue but otherwise I'm curious if there's a consideration here that I'm missing?

It is worth pointing out that there are existing polyfills of the Node.js style async `import.meta.resolve()` that works in Browsers today that have a non-zero chance of being broken by the introduction of a synchronous version of this API. For example: https://github.com/guybedford/es-module-shims#resolve. The `es-module-shims` module on npm has over 25k downloads per week and works in Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge, so there is at least *some* solid evidence that an async version of `import.meta.resolve()` would be acceptable to users.

I should also make it clear: the argument here is absolutely *NOT* that browsers should implement `import.meta.resolve()` async if they don't need it to be async. The question is why and how allowing that as an *option* is unreasonable.
It's the same reason why making `new URL()` async is unreasonable. Again, we've been over this in the previous thread.

I'll have to go dig up what other thread you're referring to as I'm not entirely clear which that is. But I'll go hunting.

> It's the same reason why making new URL() async is unreasonable.

As far as I know, no one has ever presented anything close to a reasonable use case as to why something like `new URL()` would be asynchronous. In fact, the very idea of that is obviously silly. By contrast, we've shown here (*after being [explicitly invited](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/5572#issuecomment-1034623836) in this thread* to provide feedback) that there are not only valid use cases for an async `import.meta.resolve()` but there is a workable implementation with ecosystem adoption that is *not* limited to just Node.js. It's not at all clear that it's an "obviously silly" thing.

Node.js and other platforms will do what they need to do to serve their users, yes, and I'm happy to provide feedback about what those platforms may need, especially when invited to do so. It's my opinion that the majority of users will be better served by a single API that can be implemented across all platforms -- regardless of whether those implement the actual resolution algorithm synchronously or asynchronously. I think it's absolutely possible to do so, I think it's reasonable to do so, and to answer @annevk's request for feedback: that's the API I'd like to see come out of this.

> I agree Node could have two APIs, but on the web we only have one such algorithm.

I think both Node and the web could have two APIs. If there’s a desire for a sync API, for the part of resolution that _could always be synchronous on all platforms,_ then that can be one API; and `import.meta.resolve` could be async on all platforms. I think Node would be fine with an sync `import.meta.importMapResolve` or whatever better name is found, because it explicitly isn’t intended to reproduce the entire module resolution algorithm—just this part of it, which we can define as being synchronous. On the web the two APIs could be identical under the hood with the only difference being that `resolve` returns the same result wrapped in a promise; that’s fine. From the perspective of users writing code, the APIs would have the same signatures across all platforms.

> As far as I know, no one has ever presented anything close to a reasonable use case as to why something like new URL() would be asynchronous. In fact, the very idea of that is obviously silly. 

Yes. *And the same is true for module specifier resolution.*

You want to make the loading process async? Makes perfect sense. For modules, Node can do it with loaders, or proxies for resources in general. For resources on the web, we do it with service workers. But resource identifier resolution time (e.g. relative URLs -> absolute URLs, or module specifiers -> absolute URLs) is not the place to insert that asynchronicity. It's just as silly for module specifiers as it is for URLs; it's simply not a reasonable level to add async hooks.

Well, I guess that's the crux of it then: you disagree with the way Node.js has implemented specifier resolution. And that's fine. All I would ask then that you please choose a name *other* than `import.meta.resolve()` for this new API you're introducing to avoid conflicting with the one that already exists and is implemented in the broader ecosystem. If we can't land on a single API, there's no reason to intentionally introduce a conflicting one with the same name (and given that Node.js' implementation already exists in production releases, it doesn't make sense to force them to change the name to avoid conflict)
I'm not willing to let a "stability 1: experimental" Node.js API make the web's APIs worse.

> I'm not willing to let a "stability 1: experimental" Node.js API make the web's APIs worse.

Whether or not renaming the function makes "the web's [Browsers] APIs worse" is purely subjective. Is there a particular reason this *must* be named `resolve()` beyond your personal preference? If there is, I'm not seeing it.

There are plenty of possible alternative colors for the bike-shed.

* `const url = import.meta.url('specifier')`
* `const url = import.meta.for('specifier')`
* `const url = import.meta.specifier('specifier')`
* `const url = import.meta.relative('specifier')`

In any case, I think my feedback has run its course. Please do not intentionally introduce a new API with a built-in naming conflict with an existing one as doing so does not serve end users well (regardless of whatever our personal preferences may be).

> I'm not willing to let a "stability 1: experimental" Node.js API make the web's APIs worse.

This was brought as an argument for changing it to be synchronous in a thread we have about “Workerized JS Module Script Loading”.

> This might also be beneficial to syncify some loader hooks. For example it is seeming more and more likely Chromium wants to ship a synchronous `import.meta.resolve` while Node.js has an experimental async version to support the async resolver. Syncifying resolve would permit alignment on these specs, which is currently at risk.

_Originally posted by @guybedford in https://github.com/nodejs/loaders/issues/13#issuecomment-924509238_

If the folks working on this in Node are willing to change that implementation to be sync then that resolves the issue also. I have no particular preference for sync or async, I just don't want conflicting APIs when conflicts can be avoided.

> If the folks working on this in Node are willing to change that implementation to be sync then that resolves the issue also.

I think there’s value in having _both_ APIs: resolution that behaves according to the import maps standard, and resolution that behaves according to the current platform’s particular rules.

The original proposed name for this was `import.meta.resolveURL`. What if we go back to that, for the sync API? It has a nice rhyme with `new URL`, which suggests its sync-ness. And then `import.meta.resolve` could be async and platform-specific. So:

### `import.meta.resolveURL(specifier: string) => string`

A sync function that takes a relative specifier like `./foo.txt` and resolves it via `new URL('./foo.txt', import.meta.url)`; or a bare specifier like `somepackage/resource.json` and resolves it to a URL per a loaded import map. (In other words, the behavior described in the top post.)

Deno and Node would behave the same way. Node would only resolve bare specifiers if/when Node supports import maps.

### `import.meta.resolve(specifier: string; parent?: string) => Promise<string>`

An async function that takes a relative specifier like `./foo.txt` and resolves it via `new URL('./foo.txt', parent ?? import.meta.url)`; or a bare specifier like `somepackage/resource.json` and resolves it via the current platform’s particular module resolution algorithm.

In browsers this would just be `Promise.resolve(import.meta.resolveURL(specifier))`. Node would do its legacy resolution algorithm, possibly influenced by custom loaders. Deno could choose however they’d like to implement this.

<hr />

I understand that it’s frustrating to amend a design to accommodate concerns outside of WHATWG’s scope, and I get that it probably feels redundant to have two APIs when browsers only need one. However I think there’s a lot of value to developers in this approach: all platforms would be able to implement _both_ of these APIs, with the same signatures, and they would behave as expected. When what’s important is that the _algorithm_ for resolution is cross-platform, `resolveURL` could be used; when what’s important is that the _result_ matches `import`’s resolution for the current platform, `resolve` could be used.

If this approach is acceptable, in the short term all that needs to change is that `resolve` would rename to `resolveURL` in this PR. I or someone else could open a new PR to propose the async `import.meta.resolve`. In the medium term there would probably be a period when browsers support only `resolveURL` and Node supports only `resolve`, and that’s okay; at least there’s a path for eventual parity, and the platforms would not be in conflict. I think there’s a lot of value in that.

To ensure better coordination going forward, shall we create whatwg/js-hosts as a somewhat informal place to document and coordinate cross-host JS development? We could document the APIs that are shared, different, what the general principles around using names are/should be in different places, etc. cc @codehag @bakkot

For this specific case, given that the `Node.js` API is still marked experimental, is there no way we cannot reuse that name? The alternatives suggested so far are not exactly elegant and don't really match our mental model of this space. We could maybe have something more verbose such as `resolveSpecifier`, but that seems awkward and might also lead to long term confusion for `Node.js` users.

I really like @annevk's suggestion of a whatwg/js-hosts coordination place. It could serve as a place for discussing lots of these sorts of things, including both clear overlaps like `import.meta`, but also things like recording decisions on https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/pull/1392. I'd imagine a different rough-consensus policy which is more like "no browsers strongly object, 2+ implementers of any sort are in favor" which would allow us to document something like "`import.meta.serverSideThing` has this group's stamp of approval" (even though it will never be in browsers) or "`Response.json()` has this group's stamp of approval" (even though it's too low on browsers' current priority list to get merged).

On that collaborative note, I want to try to clarify some of what is upsetting to me about how this discussion has gone. Unilaterally shipping an API, using a name which was already proposed in a standards body for use with different semantics, is not how we prefer to work in the WHATWG. If a browser did that, it would be very frowned upon, and we would strongly discount that browser's preferences in future standards discussions. And indeed, we would expect that browser to swallow the cost of migrating their users from their nonstandard API to any eventual standard. (To pick a couple of examples, Chrome's migration from Chrome-only web components v0 APIs, to cross-browser web components v1 APIs. Or, Safari's migration from Safari-only `const()` CSS syntax, to cross-browser `env()` CSS syntax.)

I was under the impression that [Stability: 1 - Experimental](https://nodejs.org/dist/latest-v17.x/docs/api/documentation.html#stability-index): "The feature is not subject to Semantic Versioning rules. Non-backward compatible changes or removal may occur in any future release. Use of the feature is not recommended in production environments." Node.js APIs would not be a danger to this sort of collaboration. I.e., they would be similar to things like Chrome's origin trials or other browsers' flagged features, which are used for gathering feedback but are not the sort of collaboration-hostile early-shipping I mentioned above. But a lot of the rhetoric above indicates that Node.js is not only unwilling to change, but they want to prevent browsers from shipping an API with the same name, which is exactly the opposite of the kind of experimentation we want at this stage in discussions.

I realize that norms are different across different communities, and some folks here may not be used to working in such a fashion. But I don't think that gives a free pass. I think it's just a sign we should try to do better about communicating these norms. And again, I think the kind of repo @annevk mentions would be a great place for that.

I think a coordination group sounds great. Sign me up!

Re Node’s `import.meta.resolve`, I think there are differing opinions represented on this thread; Node isn’t speaking with one voice on the matter, although we could. With @guybedford I’ve added this topic to tomorrow’s meeting of the Node loaders team; see https://github.com/nodejs/loaders/issues/64#issuecomment-1037627242. @domenic or @annevk or other interested parties are welcome to attend. I think it’s worth discussing on the Node side whether we _could_ change this API to be sync, and what would be the consequences of doing so.

On that point, it _is_ experimental, and we change experimental APIs all the time. I wouldn’t treat that as a blocking concern. The larger collision concern in my mind is that @guybedford’s [es-module-shims](https://github.com/guybedford/es-module-shims#resolve) is already out in the world and in use in production by apparently thousands of sites. Perhaps it’s not at the level of `String.prototype.contains` that was in wide use due to MooTools and led to the choice of `String.prototype.includes` as the name for that API, but it’s at least a consideration.

On the broader point though I think what this discussion is getting at is that we _want_ a way to do cross-platform resolution. I want to be able to do `import.meta.resolve('lodash')` and get something like `file:///.../node_modules/lodash/index.js` in Node and something like `https://.../lodash.js` in a browser. That has a lot of value. Maybe the way to achieve that is for all the platforms to agree to support sync resolution. Maybe it’s to agree to have `import.meta.resolve` be the lowest common denominator (the async function) and a separate function be the faster sync version for platforms that support sync resolution. I don’t know. Speaking at least for myself, though, with regard to the naming, I want `import.meta.resolve` to be the name of the universal one. If there must be two, `resolve` should be the one that can be used everywhere.

Building on what @guybedford wrote, @bmeck thinks he knows of a way where we could implement a sync `import.meta.resolve` while preserving our async Loaders API `resolve` hook, by moving the loaders off the main thread. This would seem to be the best of all worlds, as it would allow convergence with a sync browser `import.meta.resolve` API while preserving the ability of custom loaders to register async `resolve` hooks.

The method to “syncify” the async resolution for `import.meta.resolve` may raise some eyebrows, however, so the backup plan in case that doesn’t pass code review would be to change the Loaders API to make our `resolve` hook sync. Doing _that_ might upset other folks, however, as there are legitimate use cases for async resolution, at least in Node: resolving a specifier like `pkg/entry.js` where `pkg` is a `.tar.gz` file and needs to be extracted first, for example, is one that came up in our discussion today. Things like Yarn Plug-n-Play that use memory caches for dependencies might make file system or network calls to get those dependencies from their cache, and potentially download/extract dependencies if they’re not already in the cache. So proposing a change for the `resolve` loader hook to become sync would also need to involve discussions with those teams, to confirm that alternate solutions could be found for their tools to do what they need to do while resolution overall is sync.

> would the loaders team be ok with introducing a differently named method than `import.meta.resolve()` that can be implemented adjacent to the blocking `import.meta.resolve()` defined here, or is the expectation such that we would need a single resolve implementation?

From @domenic’s comments above, we assume that Whatwg has decided to ship a sync `import.meta.resolve` no matter what Node does. Therefore our options are either to support it or not; if we can’t provide a sync `import.meta.resolve` with the same signature as browsers, I think we need to just remove ours and have it be a missing API. We can ship something like `import { resolve } from 'node:module'` for our version. And since Whatwg’s decision doesn’t seem to depend on anything from Node, it doesn’t matter how long Node may take to work through the steps I outlined above.

If Whatwg _were_ willing to consider potentially shipping an async `import.meta.resolve`, then it would be worth waiting on the outcome of Node’s efforts. If both of the options I listed above for Node supporting a sync `import.meta.resolve` fail, then that would mean that the only way to achieve compatibility between platforms would be for Whatwg to ship the async `import.meta.resolve`.

I think it is likely that one or the other of the two options I listed above will be acceptable and get merged into Node. If it’s the latter option, where we need to make our `resolve` loader look sync, then we end up closing off some use cases (like Yarn PnP) in the interest of compatibility, _unless_ those loaders can pull off the same [`Atomics.wait` trick](https://github.com/babel/babel/blob/e77e3de402693a216088cb75cdf6a245cfd7d0f8/packages/babel-register/src/worker-client.js#L69-L85) for syncifying async code that @bmeck was suggesting in the first option. Since the `Atomics.wait` would be in userland code rather than Node, it wouldn’t require any approval from the Node team; it would just need to actually work. Getting to that point, where we have a sync `resolve` hook merged into Node that the Yarn team could test against, will take a considerable amount of time; so again it all boils down to whether Whatwg wants to wait to see what Node can accommodate or if they’d prefer to ship this API regardless of what happens on the Node side.

To add to this, please read [this detailed comment](https://github.com/nodejs/loaders/issues/64#issuecomment-1140251730) about the downsides of Node making `resolve` sync. This is the kind of user feedback we will be dealing with if we make this change. These all strike me as very reasonable use cases, though mostly more for command-line programs than browser web apps; and I’m not sure if there will be other ways to solve these problems without an async `resolve`. https://github.com/nodejs/loaders/issues/83 is an attempt to address this, but as a new API it would be a deviation from a cross-platform standard.

From my perspective, that comment displays some fundamental confusion between the resolve phases (a string operation) and the fetch phases (which includes things like checking for existence, permissions, network requests, etc.)

> From my perspective, that comment displays some fundamental confusion between the resolve phases (a string operation) and the fetch phases (which includes things like checking for existence, permissions, network requests, etc.)

In Node, the resolve “phase” includes disk operations. Going back to CommonJS, `require.resolve('foo')` will search the hard disk for a package named `foo`, first in local `node_modules`, then globally, etc. [This shipped over ten years ago](https://nodejs.org/api/modules.html#requireresolverequest-options). So I don’t think it’s unreasonable for users to think of these things as appropriate to occur within `resolve`. Deciding _what to resolve to_ takes disk operations in Node; it’s not just a string operation. [ESM resolution](https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html#resolution-algorithm) behaves largely the same way, though without automatic extension resolution.

> From my perspective, that comment displays some fundamental confusion between the resolve phases (a string operation) and the fetch phases (which includes things like checking for existence, permissions, network requests, etc.)

Hi @domenic — sorry for this being quite a delayed reply (I wasn't aware of this thread which linked to my other comment)

I'd like to clarify the use-case which led me to my other comment, which should help explain the bits which you think of as confusion on my part:

In NodeJS's current system, these imports could all resolve to the same file:

```js
import 'bar';
import 'bar/index'; // or something else depending on bar's package.json
import './node_modules/bar/index.js';
```

And `import 'bar';` from a sibling module might be referencing the _same_ `bar`, or a different `bar`, depending on the file layout (specifically: which `node_modules` folder(s) `bar` lives in).

It's important to know all that _before_ loading the module, because if they resolve to the same thing, we need to use the same instance of that module (e.g. so that any user-land global state is truly global). Once we get to the point of actually loading the module, it's too late. So we need `resolve` to detect that these are all the same thing and return one consistent URI for them (e.g. `file:///wherever/node_modules/bar/index.js`).

Now you may say that's a problem with NodeJS's `import` being too permissive in the specifiers it accepts, but the ability to use named imports is quite important for sharing dependencies while avoiding version conflicts. It's also pretty well established and shared with highly popular tools like WebPack and Rollup, which makes it very popular with destined-for-browser code (pre-bundling).

Import maps have of course been created to fill this need in the browser (with the intent being that all this information which was previously gathered by polling the filesystem is now available declaratively in-advance), but they are at an early stage (and only implemented in one runtime), so I for one cannot yet rely on them for this use-case (even in an experimental capacity).

I could also imagine a future need to lazy-load or even dynamically-generate import maps, especially in local environments like Node where the number of entries could be _vast_. Even in-browser I could imagine the need to fetch (sub) import maps on-demand once nesting / combining of maps gets more specced out, which would make the `resolve` call into something more interesting.

---

My preference (as a userspace developer with a vested interest in keeping parity between browsers and NodeJS) is that `import.meta.resolve` be defined as asynchronous. I understand that making it asynchronous has the downside that it will not be usable in synchronous contexts, but since asynchronous APIs are already quite common (and in particular used by `import()`), this doesn't seem likely to cause any problems. If it really truly _must not_ be asynchronous, then it should be unavailable to userspace code until import maps are more mature and widely used, because making it synchronous now will cause problems if it turns out that module resolution is not always going to be a simple string operation (even in-browser).
FYI, the compartments proposal at TC39 (https://github.com/tc39/proposal-compartments) also defines specifier resolving as being a synchronous operation. (grep for `resolveHook`).
